title: Cycle Capacity Reservation Bands and Fallthrough Queues - Runbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Provide an operational runbook that product, engineering and SRE teams can use during cycle planning and mid-cycle triage to reserve staffing for critical commitments while allowing controlled opportunistic work. The runbook introduces two primary constructs: (1) Capacity Reservation Bands — named staffing slices (Commit Band, Buffer Band, Float Band) with clear allocation rules and rebalancing thresholds; (2) Fallthrough Queues — lightweight routing for unplanned urgent work that can be absorbed without derailing the Commit Band.

Why this ticket: teams repeatedly sacrifice predictability when urgent work arrives mid-cycle. We need a lightweight, repeatable protocol to: ensure committed OKRs get predictable coverage, reduce ad-hoc scope emergency drift, and give a clear mechanism for when/how to cut scope or borrow from buffers. This is intended to align with OKR cadence and reduce discussion friction during weekly cadence checkpoints.

Key outcomes / acceptance criteria:
- A one-page runbook that PMs, Eng managers, and SREs can read and apply during planning and mid-cycle rebalances.
- Clear definitions for Commit Band (>=60% of team capacity for cycle-level OKRs), Buffer Band (10-25% for anticipated cross-team work), Float Band (0-20% for exploratory/low-risk tasks).
- A three-step mid-cycle rebalancing decision flow (Assess impact, Offer compensating scope cut, Execute fallback) with escalation path.
- Instrumentation plan: dashboards for band utilization, number of fallthrough queue events, and % of cycle work moved.
- Rollout checklist and training sessions for PMs and Eng managers in two pilot orgs.

Constraints & trade-offs:
- Committing a larger Commit Band improves predictability but reduces room for important cross-team unblockers. We recommend starting with conservative Commit Band percentages and tuning after two cycles.
- Buffer Band increases context switches if overused; require a short approval gating rule for Buffer Band pulls.
- Fallthrough Queues must be time-boxed (e.g., 3 sprint days) before formal escalation to avoid permanent scope creep.

Runbook highlights (quick reference):
- During planning: PMs propose Commit Band targets per team tied to OKR impact. Eng managers confirm capacity and flag long-lead dependencies.
- Weekly cadence check: bands reported in the cycle dashboard; any Buffer Band usage >50% triggers a triage meeting with the PM, Eng manager, and SRE.
- Mid-cycle urgent work: try to route into Float Band first. If Float Band exhausted, fallthrough queue accepts up to 2 high-severity items/week with explicit compensating scope cut identified.
- Scope cut hierarchy: (1) Deferred non-OKR tickets, (2) Lower-priority roadmap items, (3) Exploratory spikes.

Instrumentation & KPIs:
- Band utilization heatmap (per team) updated daily.
- Number of fallthrough queue events per week. Target: <=1/week per org during pilots.
- % of committed OKR story points completed on time. Target: +15% improvement vs baseline.
- Mean time to escalate (fallthrough -> formal scope cut). Target: <72 hours.

Rollout plan:
1) Pilot with two product orgs (Infra & Console) for 2 cycles (2026-W11..W18).
2) Run training workshop and distribute one-page runbook; create cycle dashboard templates.
3) Collect telemetry and adjust band percentages after pilot cycles.
4) Formalize as part of standard cycle planning templates and template PRs.

Open questions / requests for input:
- SRE: is the suggested 72-hour escalation acceptable given on-call rotations? (see dependency ENG-84231 - autoscaler experiment).
- People Ops: should we include a wellbeing guardrail preventing >20% of devs being assigned to Buffer/Float simultaneously?
- Finance: buy-in for measuring cost impact of Buffer Band staffing drift (for Dedicated customer-facing work).
